title: Orthonormal bases
objectives: Use orthonormal bases and orthogonal matrices to simplify calculations.
Find coordinates in an orthonormal basis by dot products.

screens.prose: Here $\mathbf{q}_1 = (0.6, 0.8)$ and $\mathbf{q}_2 = (-0.8, 0.6)$. The caption shows $c_1 = \mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}$ and $c_2 = \mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}$. The dashed box builds $c_1\mathbf{q}_1 + c_2\mathbf{q}_2$ from them.
screens.question: Drag $\mathbf{v}$ around. Where does the corner $c_1\mathbf{q}_1 + c_2\mathbf{q}_2$ of the dashed box land?

options.text: Exactly on the head of $\mathbf{v}$, wherever $\mathbf{v}$ is

options.why: Try $\mathbf{v} = (2, 1)$, which lies along neither: the corner still lands on its head.

options.text: Somewhere along $\mathbf{v}$, but short of its head
options.why: Dot products with unit vectors do not shrink anything. The corner sits on the head itself.

hints.text: Drag $\mathbf{v}$ to $(3, -2)$ and compare the two arrow heads.

feedback.correct: The two dot products rebuild $\mathbf{v}$ exactly.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag to two or three places and compare the corner with the head of the arrow.

explain.text: Wherever you dragged $\mathbf{v}$, the corner landed on it. So the dot products $c_1 = \mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}$ and $c_2 = \mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ in the basis $\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2$. No equations had to be solved.

screens.prose: Your basis has two properties: each vector has length 1, and the two are orthogonal. Such a basis is **orthonormal**. Below, its vectors are the columns of $\mathbf{Q}$, and the rows of $\mathbf{Q}^T$.
screens.question: Fill in the three dot products.

hints.text: Multiply matching entries and add.

feedback.correct: 1, 0 and 1: unit lengths and a right angle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply matching entries of the two vectors and add.

explain.text: Your three dot products are the entries of $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$, because row $i$ of $\mathbf{Q}^T$ is $\mathbf{q}_i$. So orthonormal columns mean $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$. A square $\mathbf{Q}$ with this property is an **orthogonal matrix**.

screens.prose: With an orthonormal basis, coordinates are dot products. Take $\mathbf{v} = (5, 5)$.
screens.question: Find $c_1$ and $c_2$ with $\mathbf{v} = c_1\mathbf{q}_1 + c_2\mathbf{q}_2$.

hints.text: $c_1 = \mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}$ and $c_2 = \mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot each basis vector with $(5, 5)$.

byKey.r1c1: $c_2 = \mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v} = -0.8(5) + 0.6(5)$. If you wrote 5, you copied the standard coordinate of $\mathbf{v}$.

explain.text: Check: $7(0.6, 0.8) - (-0.8, 0.6) = (5, 5)$. In matrix form you computed $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{v}$, solving $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{v}$. So $\mathbf{Q}^T$ is the inverse of $\mathbf{Q}$, found with no elimination.

screens.prose: Multiplying by $\mathbf{Q}$ turns the coordinates $\mathbf{x} = (3, 4)$ into the vector $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x} = 3\mathbf{q}_1 + 4\mathbf{q}_2$.
screens.question: What is the length $|\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}|$?

hints.text: Compute $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x} = 3(0.6, 0.8) + 4(-0.8, 0.6)$ first.
$\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x} = (-1.4, 4.8)$. Its squared length is $1.96 + 23.04$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the coordinates of the vector first, then use Pythagoras.

byKey.add: You added the coordinates 3 and 4. Lengths combine by Pythagoras, since $\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$ are orthogonal: $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2}$.
byKey.no-root: That is $|\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}|^2$. Take the square root.

explain.text: $\mathbf{Q}$ kept the length at 5: it rotated $\mathbf{x}$ and changed nothing else. Angles between vectors are kept as well.

screens.prose: Four matrices. $\mathbf{R}$ turns the plane through 90° and $\mathbf{P}$ reorders three coordinates. $\mathbf{S}$ is a shear, and $\mathbf{T}$ stretches one axis and squeezes the other.
screens.question: Which are orthogonal matrices? Select all that apply.

options.why: A shear keeps area, since its determinant is 1, but not lengths. Its second column $(1, 1)$ has length $\sqrt{2}$.
$\mathbf{T}$ also has determinant 1, yet it doubles $(1, 0)$. Orthogonal needs unit, orthogonal columns.

hints.text: Check each matrix's columns: unit length, and orthogonal to each other?
Look at the second column of $\mathbf{S}$.
$\mathbf{R}$: $(0, 1)$ and $(-1, 0)$. $\mathbf{P}$: three different unit axes. $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{T}$ have a column of length other than 1.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{R}$ rotates and $\mathbf{P}$ permutes: both have orthonormal columns.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test the columns of each matrix for unit length and right angles.

explain.text: The columns of $\mathbf{R}$ and of $\mathbf{P}$ are orthonormal, so both keep every length. $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{T}$ keep area, since their determinants are 1, but they stretch some vectors. Rotations and permutations are the standard orthogonal matrices.

screens.prose: $\mathbf{Q}$ can be tall. Its columns $\mathbf{q}_1 = \tfrac13(1, 2, 2)$ and $\mathbf{q}_2 = \tfrac13(2, 1, -2)$ are orthonormal, so $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}_2$. Now multiply the other way round.
screens.question: What is the top-left entry of $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T$?

hints.text: Entry $(1, 1)$ of $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T$ is row 1 of $\mathbf{Q}$ dotted with itself.
Row 1 of the tall matrix.
Row 1 is $(\tfrac13, \tfrac23)$, so the entry is $\tfrac19 + \tfrac49$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot the first row of the tall matrix with itself.

byKey.identity: You assumed $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T = \mathbf{I}$ as well. Row 1 of $\mathbf{Q}$ dotted with itself is $\tfrac19 + \tfrac49 = \tfrac59$.
byKey.one-column: You used only $\mathbf{q}_1$. Row 1 of $\mathbf{Q}$ is $(\tfrac13, \tfrac23)$, so both columns contribute: $\tfrac19 + \tfrac49$.

explain.text: $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ dots columns with columns, but $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T$ dots rows with rows, and these rows are not orthonormal. $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T$ is 3 by 3 with rank 2, so it cannot be $\mathbf{I}_3$. Level 2 shows it projects onto the plane of the columns.

screens.prose: A classmate builds $\mathbf{Q}$ from the orthogonal columns $(1, 1)$ and $(-1, 1)$. To solve $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{b}$ they write $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$.
screens.question: What is $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$, and is the classmate right?

options.why: You checked only that the columns are orthogonal, the zeros off the diagonal. The diagonal holds each column's squared length: $1^2 + 1^2 = 2$.

options.text: The zero matrix, since the columns are orthogonal
options.why: Orthogonal columns zero the entries off the diagonal only. Each column dotted with itself gives its squared length, 2.

hints.text: Entry $(i, j)$ of $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ is column $i$ dotted with column $j$.
Dot the first column with itself.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute all four entries of the product, the diagonal included.

byKey.ident: You checked only the zeros off the diagonal. Each diagonal entry is a column's squared length, here 2, so the columns are orthogonal but not unit.

explain.text: Orthogonal columns give a diagonal $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$, but only unit columns give $\mathbf{I}$. Divide each column by its length $\sqrt{2}$ and the classmate's formula works.

screens.prose:
Your screens add up to three rules for a matrix with orthonormal columns:

$$\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}, \qquad \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{v}, \qquad |\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}| = |\mathbf{x}|$$

When $\mathbf{Q}$ is square it is an orthogonal matrix, and $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^T$.
screens.question: $\mathbf{Q}$ is a 3 by 3 orthogonal matrix. How do you solve $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$?

options.text: By elimination: the shortcut only works in two dimensions
options.why: $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$ holds in any size, so the transpose is the inverse for 3 by 3 too.
Multiplying by $\mathbf{Q}$ again rotates further. You need $\mathbf{Q}^T$ to undo $\mathbf{Q}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which matrix undoes an orthogonal matrix?

explain.text: $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{b}$, and the left side is $\mathbf{x}$. Each entry is a dot product, $x_i = \mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{b}$, exactly as on your first screen.

screens.prose: You saw $|\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}| = |\mathbf{x}| = 5$. Prove it for any $\mathbf{Q}$ with orthonormal columns.
screens.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: $|\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}|^2 = (\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x})^T(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x})$, since a squared length is a vector's transpose times itself
$= \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}$, since the transpose of a product reverses the order
$= \mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{I}\mathbf{x}$, since the columns of $\mathbf{Q}$ are orthonormal

hints.text: Write the squared length with a transpose first.
Then reverse the transpose, use $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$, and simplify.

feedback.correct: Each line follows from the one before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the squared length, open the transpose, then use orthonormality.

byKey.l2: Reversing a transpose needs the transpose written out first.
byKey.l3: $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ appears only after the transpose is reversed.

explain.text: The proof uses only $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$, so it holds for a tall $\mathbf{Q}$ too. The same lines give $(\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}) \cdot (\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}$, so angles are kept as well.

screens.prose: Daily returns of two stocks, in %, move together. Rotate them into $f_1 = \mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{r}$ and $f_2 = \mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{r}$, where $\mathbf{r} = (r_A, r_B)$. For this data $\mathbf{q}_1$ and $\mathbf{q}_2$ are the **principal component** directions.
screens.question: Fill in day 1's $f_1$ and $f_2$.

hints.text: Each $f$ is a dot product with day 1's returns $(2.2, 4.6)$.
Day 1's point.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Dot each direction with $(2.2, 4.6)$.

explain.text: $f_1$ swings by ±5 and $f_2$ by only ±1, and $\sum f_1 f_2 = 5 - 5 - 5 + 5 = 0$, so the new series are uncorrelated. The total sum of squares is kept: $38.56 + 65.44 = 104 = 100 + 4$. An orthogonal change of basis keeps total variance; it only shares it out differently.

ideas: Orthonormal columns mean $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$. For a square $\mathbf{Q}$ that makes $\mathbf{Q}^{-1} = \mathbf{Q}^T$, with no elimination.
In an orthonormal basis the coordinates are dot products: $c_i = \mathbf{q}_i \cdot \mathbf{v}$.
Multiplying by $\mathbf{Q}$ keeps lengths and angles, as rotations and permutations do.

formula.name: Orthogonal matrix
formula.note: For a square $\mathbf{Q}$. A tall $\mathbf{Q}$ still has $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$, but $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T \neq \mathbf{I}$.

summary.trap: Orthogonal columns that are not unit length give a diagonal $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$, not $\mathbf{I}$. Divide each column by its length first.

quiz.prose: $\mathbf{q}_1 = (0.6, 0.8)$ and $\mathbf{q}_2 = (-0.8, 0.6)$ form an orthonormal basis. Take $\mathbf{v} = (2, -1)$.
quiz.question: What is the coordinate $c_2$ in $\mathbf{v} = c_1\mathbf{q}_1 + c_2\mathbf{q}_2$?

byKey.read-entry: You copied the second standard coordinate of $\mathbf{v}$. In this basis the coordinate is $\mathbf{q}_2 \cdot \mathbf{v}$.
byKey.c1: That is $c_1 = \mathbf{q}_1 \cdot \mathbf{v}$. The question asks for $c_2$.

quiz.prose: The rotation $\mathbf{R} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 & -0.6 \\ 0.6 & 0.8 \end{pmatrix}$ is an orthogonal matrix.
quiz.question: What is $\mathbf{R}^{-1}$?

options.why: That is $\mathbf{R}$ itself. Rotating again turns further; it does not turn back.
You negated every entry. That is $\mathbf{R}$ followed by a half turn, not its inverse.
You took the reciprocal of each entry. A matrix inverse is not found entry by entry.

feedback.correct: The transpose: swap rows and columns.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For an orthogonal matrix the inverse is the transpose.

explain.text: $\mathbf{R}^T\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}$, since the columns are orthonormal: $0.8^2 + 0.6^2 = 1$ and $0.8(-0.6) + 0.6(0.8) = 0$. So $\mathbf{R}^{-1} = \mathbf{R}^T$, the turn the other way.

options.why: $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T$ has rank at most 2, so it cannot be the 3 by 3 identity.

options.text: Neither product is an identity, since $\mathbf{Q}$ is not square
options.why: $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ dots the orthonormal columns with each other, which gives $\mathbf{I}_2$ whatever the shape.
$\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ is 2 by 2: one row and one column per column of $\mathbf{Q}$.

feedback.correct: Columns are orthonormal; rows of a tall $\mathbf{Q}$ are not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the size of each product first.

explain.text: $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ is 2 by 2 and dots the columns, so it is $\mathbf{I}_2$. $\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{Q}^T$ is 3 by 3 with rank 2, so it misses $\mathbf{I}_3$. Lengths are still kept: $|\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{x}| = |\mathbf{x}|$ needs only $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}$.

quiz.question: What must you do to them to make $\mathbf{Q}$ an orthogonal matrix?

options.why: Each column has length 5, so $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q} = 25\mathbf{I}$, not $\mathbf{I}$.
You divided by the squared length. That gives columns of length $\tfrac15$.
Swapping changes the order, not the lengths. $\mathbf{Q}^T\mathbf{Q}$ is still $25\mathbf{I}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute each column's length.

explain.text: Dividing by the length 5 gives $(0.6, 0.8)$ and $(-0.8, 0.6)$, the basis from this lesson. The right angle was already there; only the lengths needed fixing.
